title: Speed-to-Dollar argumentation notes for field
content:
Purpose and intended use:
This is a field-ready note pack for AE/SDR/Product Marketing to articulate the 'speed-to-dollar' story: how Redwood converts latency and throughput advantages into measurable cost savings and UX gains for customers. Use it as:
- an internal quick reference (talking points + evidence slices)
- a lightweight experiment plan to validate claims in customer environments
- a one-page proof checklist to attach to proposals

Background summary (one-paragraph):
Customers care about two things simultaneously: perceived application responsiveness (latency) and unit cost (per-token or per-embedding spend). Redwood’s differentiated runtime and routing controls let teams reduce median and tail latency while lowering per-token compute spend through batching, caching, and model variant routing. That combination unlocks lower total cost of ownership and better conversion/engagement because UX improves at the same time.

Topline value claims (framing for pitches):
- Claim A (speed): "Sub-100ms median inference under typical chat loads; p95 < 350ms for single-turn requests" — positioning for consumer-facing, latency-sensitive experiences.
- Claim B (cost): "Reduce per-token infra spend by 20–45% on typical customer workloads via adaptive batching, KV caching, and quantized model variants."
- Claim C (speed-to-dollar): "For the same user experience, Redwood can cut monthly inference bills by 15–30% vs unmanaged single-model endpoints by combining smarter routing with cached prefixes and smaller variants for cheap flows."
Note: these are field-friendly ranges — cite lab benchmarks when asked for decimals.

Supporting proof points and how to demonstrate them quickly:
1) Live-demo script (10 minutes):
- Setup: Two identical simple chat endpoints, one served through Redwood hosted API with prefix caching enabled and one through a baseline single-endpoint provider.
- Flow: 100 scripted users (or 500 small sequential requests) with a 80/20 distribution of short vs. long prompts.
- Observable: median latency, p95 latency, tokens generated per request, and total infra CPU/GPU time.
- Expected delta: median latency down 2–3x on short prompts, p95 reduced ~30–50% if microbursts are smoothed. Cost: token infra time reduced 25–40% depending on cache hit rate.

2) Customer validation checklist (attach to PoC):
- Instrumentation enabled (traces + token-level cost)
- Typical conversation simulator (n sessions, X turns avg)
- Run: 1-hour baseline then 1-hour Redwood config with same traffic pattern
- Measure: per-hour token cost, median/p95 latency, failed requests, fallbacks used
- Decision metric: If cost drops >=10% while p95 improves or holds, classify as success.

Competitive posture (short matrix + positioning hooks):
- Competitor: Generic cloud-managed endpoint
  - Strength: simplicity, brand familiarity
  - Weakness: single-model routing, limited prefix caching, fewer optimizations for bursty chat
  - Redwood angle: "We give the same simplicity with extra runtime smarts that convert into lower unit costs for real chat workloads."
- Competitor: Self-hosted inference runtimes (open-source)
  - Strength: fine-grained control, pricing predictable for static infra
  - Weakness: ops burden, maintenance, lack of unified telemetry + model catalog
  - Redwood angle: "Get ops-light predictable economics and observability without building the control plane."
- Competitor: Specialty low-cost embeddings providers
  - Strength: cheap embedding per-unit claims
  - Weakness: often trade off latency, model freshness, or lack routing for mixed workloads
  - Redwood angle: "We match or beat per-embedding spend in real customer workloads by choosing variants and caching aggressively while preserving latency SLAs."

Message primitives and quick lines for reps:
- For engineers: "We optimize the whole request lifecycle — not just tokens — so you get fewer wasted compute cycles and lower p95 even under microbursts."
- For product leaders: "Same user experience, lower TCO — we shrink your inference bill without sacrificing responsiveness."
- For platform/security buyers: "Single API and console across hosted, dedicated, and private deploys — predictable economics plus enterprise controls."

Two-minute elevator script (concise):
"Redwood reduces both latency and per-token cost by treating inference as an operational problem: adaptive batching, smart KV+prefix caching, and model-variant routing that routes cheap models to low-complexity traffic. The result: faster experiences, lower infra spend, and easy rollouts — measurable within a 1–2 week PoC."

Objection handling (common pushbacks + counters):
- "Sounds good in lab, hard to replicate in our environment." -> Counter: "We start with a short 1–2 day instrumented run and a deterministic simulator of your traffic; our hypothesis-driven checklist isolates the variables quickly and we can run side-by-side comparisons."
- "We can build caching ourselves." -> Counter: "Caching is only part of the picture — routing, kernel-level runtime optimizations, queuing policies, and integrated observability are where we convert ops investment into predictable unit economics."
- "Lower cost probably means lower quality outputs." -> Counter: "We surface quality tradeoffs in the console, and use canary/rollout controls to ensure quality thresholds are maintained. Often cheaper variants are only used for low-risk flows (summaries, short replies)."

Evidence appendix (what to attach to customer decks):
- Short benchmark summary table (median/p95/cost delta) for three workload archetypes: search chat, transactional assistant, embeddings-heavy analytics.
- Trace screenshots demonstrating prefix cache hit rate and tokens avoided.
- Small code snippet showing how to enable KV caching + rollouts (pseudo-code) — link to docs.

Experiment ideas to validate in 72 hours:
- Microburst smoothing test: synthetic 1k requests/min bursts vs steady 200 req/min baseline; measure p95 and queue times with adaptive batching toggled.
- Cost-per-session unpacking: instrument a real session (avg tokens/session) and show how routing to cheaper variants for N% of turns changes monthly spend projection.

Suggested next deliverables for the field team:
- One-pager proof checklist (finalize and attach to proposal)
- Short notebook with synthetic runner and dashboard links for demos
- Two slides for sales deck: (1) core claim + visual of latency & cost delta, (2) quick PoC steps & success metric

Open questions for engineering to confirm before committing to quantitative claims:
- Typical cache hit rates on customer data patterns (we need realistic ranges to tighten % savings)
- Cost accounting semantics across dedicated vs hosted infra (where do infra + licensing lines fall?)
- Any new kernel or runtime features planned that would materially change ms/token under heavy sequence lengths

Notes to self (informal):
- Keep ranges conservative for external-facing slides; use optimistic numbers in internal win/loss logs.
- Avoid precise ms numbers without an attached lab bench — customers will ask for the test harness.
- Follow up with metrics team for the 6-month benchmark deck refresh (Q3).

End of brief.

Deliverable checklist (to ship this doc into a customer-ready artifact):
- [ ] Convert to 1-page sales play PDF
- [ ] Create demo notebook in repo and link in linked_artifacts
- [ ] Get engineering sign-off on benchmark phrasing
- [ ] Add to sales enablement library
summary: Field kit for articulating how latency and cost advantages translate to lower TCO and better user experience. Includes claims, quick proofs, demo checklists, competitor hooks, experiment ideas, and field deliverables.
